resources.string: Change the keyboard colours for colour blindness

This setting changes the keyboard colours. Colours that look the same to you become different.

Select the type that agrees with your vision. Deuteranopia and protanopia are the two red-green types. Deuteranopia is the most common one. Tritanopia is the blue-yellow type. Grey removes all colour.

This setting corrects the colours. It does not simulate them. It does not show you what a person with colour blindness sees. It makes the keyboard easier for you to read.
The keyboard keeps the colours of your theme
Red-green. This is the most common type
Removes all colour from the keyboard
Labels with the highest contrast on a plain black or white board

The keyboard replaces the key colours and the board colours of the theme with flat high contrast colours. Every label becomes pure black or pure white.

The keyboard keeps the accent colour of your theme. Shift and the active tools stay easy to see.

This setting replaces the colours of the selected theme while it is on.

If the key shape of the theme is None, the keys become rounded while this setting is on.
Draw a border around every key and every toolbar tool

Outlines keep the key edges easy to see when the key colour and the board colour have almost the same brightness. This helps with themes that are partly transparent, or with a background image.

The background behind each toolbar tool gets the same border, unless that background is switched off in Appearance.

A theme that has its own key border or tool outline keeps it.

If the key shape of the theme is None, the keys become rounded while this setting is on.
The keyboard makes the lines of the key labels thicker. Use this with high contrast keys on a small screen, or on a screen with low brightness.

The Braille Institute made %1$s for people with low vision or with reading difficulty. Characters that usually look the same are drawn differently. Examples are the capital I, the lowercase l and the digit 1, or the capital O and the zero.\n\nThis setting is a shortcut for the keyboard font. When you turn it off, the keyboard uses the system font again. To select another font, go to Appearance › Keyboard font.
Size of the labels on the keys
See all the fonts, or import your own font
Turn off the animation that is not necessary
Panels grow out of the button or tool name that opened them

When you open a panel such as the clipboard, emoji or a tool, it grows out of the toolbar button or the tool name you tapped, and it folds back into it when you close it. The animation is short, so it does not slow you down.
Turn this off and panels appear and disappear at once. Reduce motion also turns this off.
The selection highlight and its buttons move smoothly

While you select text with the keyboard, the highlight slides to the new selection and the buttons of the selection bar come in one after the other.
Turn this off and the selection and its buttons change at once. Reduce motion also turns this off.
Keys flip to the new language when you switch

When you switch language, each key that shows a different letter in the new language flips over to it. Keys that stay the same hold still, so you can see what changed.
Off by default, because the plain switch is the fastest. Only a language switch animates. Changing to symbols or numbers never does. Reduce motion also turns this off.
Fixes and translations move into place

In the grammar tool, a fix you apply crosses out the old words and slides the new ones in, and the list of problems closes up around it. In the translate tool, the part of the translation that changed fades in while the words that stayed hold still, and the language swap button turns.
Off by default, because these tools are for getting text out fast. Reduce motion also turns this off.
Opening one more section on a screen closes the one you used least recently

Some screens, like the theme editor, have sections that open and close with a press on their heading. Pick a number and a screen keeps at most that many open: opening another closes the one you went longest without opening or touching. The section you just opened and the one you were last changing something in are the ones that stay.\n\nNo limit keeps every section you open until you close it.
The alternates popup as it used to be, with nothing moving under your finger

When you hold a key, its alternates popup normally opens with the first alternate right over the key and the others on both sides of it, the alternate you aim at grows, and the highlight follows your finger a row above it and slides from one alternate to the next.\n\nTurn this on for the popup as it used to be. It opens where the key is, the alternates run in reading order, the highlight is on whatever alternate is under your finger, nothing grows, and the highlight jumps straight to the next alternate instead of sliding. Choosing still works the same way: slide to an alternate and lift.

This setting is for motion sensitivity. It turns off the slide and scale transitions in the keyboard toolbar and in this settings app. It also turns off the animated theme backgrounds, the blinking cursors and the pulse ring of the microphone.

The keyboard keeps the feedback that gives you information: the key preview bubble, the colour of a pressed key and the gesture trail. Without this feedback the keyboard is more difficult to use.

The cursors and the microphone ring stay visible. They hold still.

When you turn animations off for the whole device, in Accessibility or in the developer options, the keyboard follows that and behaves as if this setting is on. This setting stays yours: it turns motion off for the keyboard only, and it leaves the rest of your device as it is.
A coloured icon beside every setting and screen name
A setting\'s icon and name move into the screen it opens

Turn this off if these settings screens are slow to open on your phone. Moving a setting\'s icon and name into the screen it opens makes each screen take more work to draw, and some slower phones show that as a stutter. With this off, a screen opens with the plain slide, and it draws faster.\n\nThis changes only these settings screens. It does nothing to the keyboard. When Reduce motion is on, these transitions are already off.

Turn this off for plain rows that show only words, as in earlier versions of the app. Some people find a list of words easier to read than a column of coloured icons.\n\nThis changes only these settings screens. The icons of the keyboard and of its tools stay as they are.
A small button on every settings screen that opens the keyboard with a field to type in

The button sits in the bottom corner of every settings screen. Tap it and a text field opens above the real keyboard, so you can try a change on the screen where you made it, without going back to another app. Tap the button again, or hide the keyboard, to close the field. It stays open while you move between settings screens.\n\nScreens that already show a keyboard of their own, such as the theme editor, don\'t show the button. Turn this off if you don\'t want the button on your screens.
Type here to try your changes
A star at the top of every settings screen that lists your favourite settings

Tap the star at the top of any settings screen to see your favourites, and tap one to go there. In the list, Add this screen pins the screen you are on. To pin one setting, touch and hold it and choose Add to favourites.\n\nThe star is filled on a screen that is already a favourite. Turn this off if you don\'t want the button. Your favourites are kept and come back when you turn it on again.
Nothing here yet. Add the screen you are on, or touch and hold a setting and choose Add to favourites.
How the keyboard announces the keys

Off: the keys have no spoken name. A screen reader cannot find the keyboard.

Labels: every key has a spoken name. Punctuation keys also have a name, for example "full stop" and "at sign". You type by direct touch as usual. Use this if you start a screen reader only sometimes, or if you use switch access.

Explore by touch: this is the standard keyboard behaviour with a screen reader. Move your finger to hear each key, then activate the key to type it. This changes the keys only while TalkBack runs. When TalkBack is off, the keyboard types as usual.

Gestures: the keyboard keeps its own touch handling while TalkBack runs. The spacebar cursor slide, the backspace word swipe, glide typing and handwriting continue to work. Each key speaks when you touch it, and types when you lift your finger. This mode needs the keyboard gestures service below. Without that service this mode acts like Explore by touch.
The keys have no spoken name
Every key has a spoken name. You type by direct touch
Move your finger to hear a key, then activate it to type
The keyboard gestures continue to work while TalkBack runs
On. The keys get your touches. TalkBack keeps the rest of the screen
While TalkBack runs, its own gestures replace the spacebar swipes and the press and hold alternates of the keyboard.

The pass-through service marks the key grid to bypass the touch handling of TalkBack. This is the only way that an app can get its own gestures there.

The service reads nothing. It receives no accessibility events. It cannot see the screen content. It covers the keys only. TalkBack explores the suggestion strip, the toolbar and every panel as usual, and also the rest of Android.

Inside the key grid TalkBack does not speak. The keyboard announces each key when you press it. When you move your finger from one key to another, the keyboard does not announce the new key. The keyboard speaks a key when you touch it, and types the key when you lift your finger.
Off. The keyboard accepts every press
The keyboard ignores a second press of the same key for this time

This setting is for hand tremor or spasticity. After a key registers, the keyboard discards a second press of that key inside this time. One press that you want does not become two characters.

The keyboard filters repeats of the same key only. You can always type two different keys quickly.

Increase the time until the double letters stop. If the time is too long, the keyboard also discards double letters that you want, for example "ll" and "ee".
How long you hold a key before its alternate keys open
Taller keys and wider gaps are easier to press accurately
Confirm each key press with vibration or with sound
